entries.mechanism: Contributing specular paths form a manifold in path space defined by half-vector constraints (half-vector = normal at each specular vertex); a Newton-style iteration using only local differential geometry walks along it. Glossy chains are handled by 'offset manifolds' parallel to the specular manifold, since their integrand 'has its energy concentrated in a thin band near the specular manifold'.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing stored.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not applicable; the constraint is local geometry so it holds after any edit.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Directly targeted: specular, near-specular and glossy chains by the same algorithm. The paper stresses that 'nearly specular paths involving glossy materials ... can be more problematic' because they elude special mechanisms for ideal specular.
entries.cost_claims: Evaluated by equal-time comparison against prior MCMC methods; no closed-form cost.
entries.limitation: MCMC (correlated samples, needs seeding); requires differentiable geometry.
entries.relevance: Quantifies the dimensionality loss: each specular vertex removes two dimensions from path space, so the sharp family lives on a lower-dimensional set that uniform angular sampling or binning hits with vanishing measure.

entries.work: Zeltner, Georgiev, Jakob, 'Specular Manifold Sampling for Rendering High-Frequency Caustics and Glints'
entries.mechanism: Given two shading points, stochastically initialises a Newton manifold walk to find a specular sub-path connecting them; the set of solutions is 'discrete and finite', and an unbiased estimator of the reciprocal probability of finding each solution (basin-of-convergence area) is built by repeated trials. Generalises manifold next-event estimation (Hanika et al. 2015).
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing stored.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not applicable; purely geometric, usable inside unidirectional path tracing after any edit.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Handles reflective and refractive caustics, glints and SDS paths; a biased variant lowers variance. States the root problem: at specular interfaces the law of reflection 'drastically lowers the probability of sampling a valid configuration'.
entries.cost_claims: Glint variant 'reduces memory usage hundred-fold compared to prior work' (per preprint summary); cost per connection is several Newton walks.
entries.limitation: Cost grows with the number of solutions and specular chain length; unbiased weight estimation adds variance.
entries.relevance: The current reference for computing the light -> sharp reflector -> diffuse connection per query from geometry alone, with no stored transport; it defines the 'full transport' cost that any stored representation of that family competes with.

entries.work: Smits, Arvo, Salesin, 'An Importance-Driven Radiosity Algorithm'
entries.mechanism: Hierarchical radiosity refined by the product of two transported quantities: power from the lights and importance (the adjoint solution) from the visible surfaces, so that only interactions that matter to the image are refined.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: A view- and light-specific hierarchy of links plus radiosity and importance solutions.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not addressed; the refinement is tied to the view, lights and geometry.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Diffuse only (the glossy extension is Christensen et al. 1996 and Aupperle & Hanrahan's importance paper).
entries.cost_claims: 'Dramatic speedups' over previous radiosity algorithms for environments with detail at a wide range of scales (from a search-result summary of the abstract).
entries.limitation: View-dependent solution; diffuse.
entries.relevance: States the adjoint principle a designer must face: the resolution needed in a stored transport representation is set by what reads it. A diffuse reader tolerates coarse error; a near-mirror reader assigns high, localised importance to individual table entries.

entries.work: Hanrahan, Salzman, Aupperle, 'A Rapid Hierarchical Radiosity Algorithm'; Gortler, Schroeder, Cohen, Hanrahan, 'Wavelet Radiosity'; Smits, Arvo, Greenberg, 'A Clustering Algorithm for Radiosity in Complex Environments'
entries.mechanism: The form-factor (transport) matrix is represented hierarchically by links between patches at the coarsest level that meets an error bound (HR); wavelet radiosity shows HR is the Haar instance of projecting the kernel into a wavelet basis; clustering groups whole objects so links can exist above the input-surface level with bounded error.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: A block-sparse, multiresolution representation of the diffuse transport operator (links) plus the radiosity solution.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Links whose shaft (set of lines between the two elements) is untouched remain valid; this is what the later line-space hierarchy exploits.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Excluded: Lambertian environments only.
entries.cost_claims: HR: at most O(n) blocks vs n^2 form factors. Wavelet radiosity: linear-time algorithms. Clustering: initial linking O(s log s) time and O(s) space instead of O(s^2), about two orders of magnitude speed-up on moderate scenes.
entries.limitation: The linear-complexity argument rests on kernel smoothness between well-separated elements; visibility discontinuities and near-contact pairs force refinement.
entries.relevance: The classical proof that a source-independent transport operator compresses well hierarchically when the kernel is smooth - and the baseline against which glossy and near-contact transport break the compression.

entries.work: Lischinski, Tampieri, Greenberg, 'Discontinuity Meshing for Accurate Radiosity'
entries.mechanism: Object-space algorithm that computes the loci of radiance discontinuities caused by an area source and occluders in a diffuse polyhedral scene and places mesh element boundaries exactly on them.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: A geometry- and source-dependent mesh aligned with visibility discontinuities.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: The discontinuity loci move with any source or occluder motion, so the mesh must be recomputed for the affected source/occluder pairs.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Not handled (diffuse); addresses the other source of sharp spatial structure, visibility.
entries.cost_claims: Not retrieved.
entries.limitation: Combinatorial growth of discontinuity surfaces with scene complexity; primary sources only in practice.
entries.relevance: Shows that sharp spatial features of transported light are located by geometry (source x occluder edges), not by a fixed basis; a fixed patch grid cannot represent them without error at arbitrary positions.

entries.work: Chen, 'Incremental Radiosity: An Extension of Progressive Radiosity to an Interactive Image Synthesis System'
entries.mechanism: After a change (light switched, surface attribute changed, object added or moved), computes the minimum re-propagation by shooting corrective (including negative) energy for the affected interactions instead of restarting progressive radiosity.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: A converged or partially converged view-independent radiosity solution that is corrected incrementally.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Radiosity contributions between pairs whose mutual visibility is unchanged; the method must find which shooter-receiver interactions the moved object newly blocks or unblocks.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Excluded (diffuse radiosity).
entries.cost_claims: Rendering time 'may drastically' drop because modelling changes are coherent and affect only parts of an image (abstract paraphrase).
entries.limitation: Source-dependent state; correction cost grows with the number of shooters whose light reached the changed region.
entries.relevance: First statement of the dynamic-update question as 'what is the minimum recomputation after an edit', and of the answer that the dirty set is defined by changed visibility between pairs, not by the moved object alone.

entries.work: Drettakis & Sillion, 'Interactive Update of Global Illumination Using a Line-Space Hierarchy'
entries.mechanism: In hierarchical radiosity with clustering, each link is augmented with a shaft representing the set of lines through both linked elements; the links thus form an implicit hierarchy over line space, which is traversed to find links intersected by a moving object, remove subdivision no longer needed, and re-solve only the modified paths in the hierarchy.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: The link hierarchy (a hierarchical, geometry-only representation of the diffuse transport operator) with shafts, plus the current solution.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: All links whose shafts the moving object does not enter or leave; only modified links are re-evaluated and the push-pull is redone along affected branches.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Not handled; the abstract frames the work within hierarchical radiosity (diffuse).
entries.cost_claims: 'Interactive update rates' for scenes of several thousand polygons, with a quality / frame-rate trade-off by limiting traversal depth (a search summary quotes about 2-3 frames per second; that figure was not seen in the abstract).
entries.limitation: Diffuse only; number of links to test grows with scene complexity; refinement that depends on current lighting must be redone.
entries.relevance: The classical answer to 'which part of a stored transport operator does a rigid edit invalidate': index the operator by the lines it integrates over and intersect the moving object with that index.

entries.work: Granier & Drettakis, 'Incremental Updates for Rapid Glossy Global Illumination'
entries.mechanism: Unified algorithm: hierarchical radiosity with clustering for diffuse transport and particle tracing for non-diffuse transport; on an edit, a dynamic spatial structure limits the particles that must be re-emitted, and the line-space hierarchy updates the diffuse part. Caustics are reconstructed either on the radiosity mesh or in dedicated caustic textures when high frequencies appear.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Diffuse link hierarchy and solution; stored particle paths / caustic textures for the non-diffuse part.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Diffuse links outside the moved object's shafts; particles whose paths do not cross the changed region. Affected particles are re-shot.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Non-diffuse transport is taken out of the finite-element operator altogether and carried by light-side particle tracing with its own incremental mechanism.
entries.cost_claims: Rapid local modification; 'quasi-interactive' updates with slight quality loss during motion (from search-result abstract text).
entries.limitation: Two separate mechanisms with separate invalidation logic; the non-diffuse part is stored per light state, not as an operator.
entries.relevance: The closest classical precedent to the exact problem (glossy GI kept valid under local geometry edits): its answer was a split in which only the diffuse part is a reusable geometric operator and the sharp part is recomputed by selective shooting.

entries.work: Dachsbacher, Stamminger, Drettakis, Durand, 'Implicit Visibility and Antiradiance for Interactive Global Illumination'
entries.mechanism: Reformulates the rendering equation with an unoccluded transport operator and propagates an extra directional quantity, antiradiance, emitted backwards from every surface to cancel light that wrongly passed through it; solved with spatial x directional finite elements (e.g. 128 direction bins) and hierarchical links, on the GPU.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: A hierarchy of unoccluded links (pure pairwise geometry, no visibility) with filtered form factors.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Pairwise propagation 'does not depend on occlusion due to other objects', so after a move 'we only have to update links to and from moving objects'; with bounded motion the link hierarchy is kept and only unoccluded form factors are recomputed.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: 'For low-frequency glossy lighting, our approach can achieve a good approximation'; directional resolution limits sharpness (128 vs 512 bins visibly changes shadow blur). The symmetric iteration is not provably convergent: 'in simplified 2D examples with multiple occlusion and perfect mirror-BRDFs, eigenvalues larger than one occur ... Highly-specular BRDFs might create more problems'.
entries.cost_claims: Office scene 18,253 elements / 632,098 links at 7-10 fps for 4 iterations; glossy scenes 6-15 fps; under 140 MB GPU memory.
entries.limitation: Two coupled quantities; directional discretisation of antiradiance sets both shadow and gloss resolution; the unoccluded operator 'can create energy'.
entries.relevance: A physically exact re-partition that makes the stored operator local under rigid edits by moving visibility out of it. It shows the cost of that move: occlusion becomes a directional cancellation problem whose accuracy is again bounded by the angular basis, and stability is no longer guaranteed for sharp BRDFs.

entries.work: Arvo, 'The Role of Functional Analysis in Global Illumination' (with Arvo, Torrance, Smits, 'A Framework for the Analysis of Error in Global Illumination Algorithms', SIGGRAPH 1994)
entries.mechanism: Poses the rendering equation in terms of linear operators on infinite-dimensional function spaces; obtains operator norms from thermodynamic principles and shows common function spaces are closed under global illumination. The 1994 paper classifies error into perturbed boundary data, discretisation (projection onto a finite basis) and computation (inexact form factors / visibility, truncated iteration), with bounds for each.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing; analysis.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not applicable. (In the operator factorisation into a local reflection operator and a geometric field/propagation operator - notation recalled from memory - only the geometric factor depends on scene layout.)
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Per Soler et al. 2022, 'Arvo analyses the specific case of specular transport and explains that specular reflections result in a non-compact operator'.
entries.cost_claims: None.
entries.limitation: Bounds are worst-case norms; they do not localise error.
entries.relevance: Source of the operator vocabulary (norms below one from energy conservation, Neumann series convergence, error from projecting an operator onto a finite basis). Passivity of a learned operator is the discrete counterpart of the thermodynamic norm bound.

entries.work: Soler, Molazem, Subr, 'A Theoretical Analysis of Compactness of the Light Transport Operator'
entries.mechanism: Proves that the light transport operator T on radiance is not compact (it is a partial integral operator), even with all-Lambertian materials; the lower-dimensional radiant-exitance operator is compact only when its kernel is bounded (purely curved scenes), and its kernel is unbounded 'next to concave abutting edges, corners, and contact points between surfaces'. The global reflectance operator K is non-compact because it is the identity in space tensor a local angular operator.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing; theory.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not applicable.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Explains 'the difficulties in extending algorithms that perform well on scenes with diffuse materials to scenes with glossy materials'; says T 'does not lend itself to low-dimensional approximations except in specific cases - away from edges and diffuse surfaces'.
entries.cost_claims: None.
entries.limitation: Worst-case statement over all light distributions; says pointwise convergence still holds, so 'a well-crafted approximation ... for a specific lighting distribution' is possible.
entries.relevance: The strongest theoretical statement on the question: 'any discretization that relies on a finite-rank or nonadaptive finite-bases is susceptible to unbounded error over arbitrary light distributions'. A source-independent operator on a fixed patch x direction basis is exactly a light-agnostic finite-rank approximation; the paper also names probes and low-rank real-time GI as implicit instances. It adds that visibility discontinuities 'are not related to boundedness or compactness'.

entries.work: Durand, Holzschuch, Soler, Chan, Sillion, 'A Frequency Analysis of Light Transport'
entries.mechanism: Local spatio-angular Fourier analysis of radiance: free-space travel is a shear in the space-angle frequency domain, occlusion is a convolution by the blocker spectrum, reflection is a multiplication by the BRDF spectrum (a glossy BRDF 'band-limits' the angular signal), curvature is a shear that 'results in a transfer from the directional frequencies to the spatial frequencies'.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing; bandwidth predictions used to drive adaptive sampling (demonstrated at 0.05 shading samples per pixel on average).
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not applicable; the predictions are local functions of BRDF bandwidth, curvature, incidence angle and blocker distance, all recomputable after an edit.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Gives an approximate bound on required sampling rate that grows with BRDF angular cutoff, curvature, grazing angle and inverse distance to blockers (harmonic mean of blocker distance); 'curvature has no effect on the directional bandwidth of the outgoing light field'. The authors' FAQ notes infinite predicted bandwidth at contact points.
entries.cost_claims: Proof-of-concept only (20,000 shading samples for an 800 x 500 image).
entries.limitation: First-order, local, single-bounce derivations; worst-case blocker spectrum; not an algorithm for multi-bounce transport.
entries.relevance: Provides the quantitative rule for what a finite spatial-angular basis can carry: the angular cutoff of the sender's lobe sets a minimum angular sample density, and after travel over distance d and reflection off curved geometry that angular bandwidth reappears as spatial bandwidth on the receiver. Sampling the sender's lobe with a fixed receiver-side ray set below this rate aliases.

entries.work: Ramamoorthi & Hanrahan, 'A Signal-Processing Framework for Inverse Rendering'
entries.mechanism: Treats the reflected light field (distant lighting, convex object) as a convolution of lighting and BRDF, i.e. a product of spherical-harmonic coefficients; inverse rendering is deconvolution.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing; theory (used later to justify low-order SH for diffuse transfer).
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not applicable (no interreflection or occlusion in the model).
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: The BRDF is the filter: Lambertian keeps only the lowest orders, a mirror has a flat spectrum (no band limit). Excludes interreflection.
entries.cost_claims: None.
entries.limitation: Distant lighting, no shadows or interreflection.
entries.relevance: Gives the per-material angular bandwidth: the number of angular basis functions needed at a reflector scales with the inverse lobe width, and a mirror needs an unbounded number - so 'broad transport' and 'sharp transport' are separated by BRDF spectrum, a property known per material before any geometry is seen.

entries.work: Mahajan, Kemelmacher-Shlizerman, Ramamoorthi, Belhumeur, 'A Theory of Locally Low Dimensional Light Transport'
entries.mechanism: Uses Szego's eigenvalue theorem on canonical configurations to derive the eigenvalue spectrum of the local transport covariance: local dimensionality (number of PCA basis functions for a given accuracy) grows linearly with patch area for glossy reflection, with slope 'of the order of the bandwidth of the BRDF or shadowing transfer function', and often as sqrt(area) for simple cast shadows.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Analysis of clustered-PCA precomputed transfer; an adaptive subdivision rule and optimal block size.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not addressed (static-scene PRT).
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: 'Dimensionality increases more rapidly ... for highly specular materials or complex cast shadows, and more slowly for diffuse surfaces.' Direct transport only in the canonical analysis.
entries.cost_claims: Rendering time sub-linear in image resolution; interactive all-frequency relighting at 1024 x 1024.
entries.limitation: Local, canonical 2D/3D cases under a convolution assumption; no interreflection in the theory.
entries.relevance: Direct statement of what limits rank: rank needed over a region is about (region size) x (BRDF or visibility bandwidth). A global low-rank term therefore cannot hold a sharp sender-receiver relation over more than a small region; the rank must scale with area times lobe sharpness.

entries.work: Lessig & Fiume, 'On the Effective Dimension of Light Transport'
entries.mechanism: Characterises the effective dimension of light transport over a neighbourhood by the spectrum of the spatio-spectral concentration problem (Slepian functions): the count of significant eigenvalues is about the product of the region size and the bandlimit (a Shannon number), with a logarithmic transition band; Slepian functions give optimal local representations.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing; theory with optimal bases for band-limited transport localised to a region.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not applicable.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Assumes transport band-limited to SH order L; the dimension is of order (L+1)^2 times the fractional region size, so it grows quadratically with angular sharpness.
entries.cost_claims: None.
entries.limitation: Band-limit assumption; radially symmetric lighting in the occlusion analysis.
entries.relevance: Supplies the counting rule (space-bandwidth product) for how many coefficients a region of a spatial-angular table needs; narrowing a lobe by a factor k multiplies the count by about k^2 on the sphere.

entries.work: Many-light matrix methods: Walter et al., 'Lightcuts'; Hasan, Pellacini, Bala, 'Matrix Row-Column Sampling for the Many-Light Problem'; Hasan, Krivanek, Walter, Bala, 'Virtual Spherical Lights for Many-Light Rendering of Glossy Scenes'
entries.mechanism: Indirect light is a sum over virtual lights, i.e. the column sum of a (receiver sample x light) transfer matrix. Lightcuts clusters lights in a tree with error bounds; row-column sampling reveals the matrix structure from a few rows and columns; virtual spherical lights replace point evaluation by integration over a non-zero solid angle to remove spikes from narrow BRDF lobes and the geometry term.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing persistent across frames; a per-frame low-rank / clustered approximation of the transfer matrix.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Nothing stored, so nothing is invalidated; cost is paid per frame.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Lightcuts: instant radiosity 'cannot reproduce some types of indirect illumination (e.g., caustics)' and 'has difficulties with short range and/or glossy indirect effects'; clamping is used. VSL: 'Including glossy transport in the matrix increases its numerical rank, so we used more rows (900-1,024) and columns (5,000-15,000)'; the method is consistent but biased and 'blurs some lighting features'.
entries.cost_claims: Lightcuts: strongly sublinear in number of lights. MRCS: seconds per frame on GPU. VSL: 1-4 minutes where path tracing or photon mapping take hours.
entries.limitation: Clamping removes exactly the sharp, short-range energy; un-clamped point evaluation spikes; the VSL fix is a spatial mollifier whose radius must shrink with light count (memory-limited near 250,000 lights).
entries.relevance: Empirical confirmation of the rank limit on a transfer matrix: diffuse transport is recoverable from a few rows and columns, glossy transport raises the numerical rank and forces either many more samples or a controlled blur.

entries.work: Hasan, Pellacini, Bala, 'Direct-to-Indirect Transfer for Cinematic Relighting'
entries.mechanism: Precomputes a large linear operator that maps direct illumination on a cloud of gather samples to multi-bounce indirect illumination at view samples of a fixed viewpoint; the operator is stored as sparse matrices in a wavelet basis built over the unstructured gather cloud and applied on the GPU.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: A source-independent direct-to-indirect transfer matrix (hierarchical algorithm plus a photon-mapping variant, under three hours on one processor).
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Nothing: geometry, materials and viewpoint are fixed; only the direct lighting (arbitrary shaders) may change.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Supports 'diffuse and glossy materials' at the final (view-sample) bounce; the gather samples carry diffuse direct illumination (detail beyond the abstract recalled from memory).
entries.cost_claims: 10-20 fps relighting for scenes over 2 million polygons.
entries.limitation: Fixed view and static scene; sender side is not directional.
entries.relevance: The canonical example of the exact operator shape in question - linear, source-independent, applied to an encoding of direct light to yield higher-order light - and of its classical scope: static geometry, broad sender radiance.

entries.work: Potter, Bertone, Schorghofer, Mazarico, 'Fast hierarchical low-rank view factor matrices for thermal irradiance on planetary surfaces'
entries.mechanism: Compresses the radiosity view-factor matrix in a hierarchical off-diagonal low-rank-like format: elements are partitioned by quadtree/octree, each block is compressed by a sparse SVD, and the hierarchical matrix is assembled by dynamic programming.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: A compressed, source-independent diffuse transport (view factor) matrix reused for many time-varying right-hand sides (moving sun).
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Static geometry assumed; the matrix is reused only across changes of illumination.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Excluded (thermal / diffuse radiosity).
entries.cost_claims: Assembly in quadratic time (comparable to the dense matrix) with much less memory; compressed size and matrix-vector product scale linearly across tested tolerances.
entries.limitation: Diffuse only; assembly remains quadratic; a search-result summary of the paper notes off-diagonal blocks are not necessarily numerically low rank because of occlusion and directionality.
entries.relevance: A recent, independent confirmation outside graphics that hierarchical-matrix compression of a source-independent transport operator pays off for diffuse kernels when the operator is reused over many sources - the economic argument for an operator - with nothing said for glossy kernels.

entries.work: Loos, Antani, Mitchell, Nowrouzezahrai, Jarosz, Sloan, 'Modular Radiance Transfer'
entries.mechanism: Stores compact light-transport operators on simple proxy shapes, in low-dimensional subspaces obtained with a prior on incident lighting; the shapes' transport is 'instanced, warped and connected on-the-fly' through interfaces to approximate indirect light in large scenes.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Scene-independent, shape-dependent low-rank transport operators and interface operators.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: The per-shape operators are reused under re-arrangement of the modules; coupling is recomputed at run time from how modules are connected.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Not targeted: 'coarse-scale, distant indirect lighting effects'; low-rank subspaces.
entries.cost_claims: More than 475 fps on high-end GPUs and more than 45 fps on mobile.
entries.limitation: Approximate, low-frequency, proxy geometry; no sharp directional relations.
entries.relevance: Precedent for a reusable transport operator attached to a piece of geometry and composed with others after rearrangement, achieved by restricting the transport to low dimension.

entries.work: Hadadan, Chen, Zwicker, 'Neural Radiosity' and Zheng et al., 'NeLT: Object-oriented Neural Light Transfer'
entries.mechanism: Neural Radiosity represents the full four-dimensional radiance distribution by a network trained to minimise the norm of the rendering-equation residual, noting that classical radiosity bases 'are typically limited to representing isotropic scattering from diffuse surfaces'. NeLT is 'a novel modular neural representation of the dynamic light transportation between an object and the environment', composed explicitly across objects.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Neural Radiosity: a scene- and lighting-specific radiance field. NeLT: per-object neural light-transfer functions.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Neural Radiosity: nothing (the solution is for one scene state). NeLT: per-object transfer is reused as objects move, with inter-object effects composed at run time (from the abstract and a search-result summary).
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Neural Radiosity demonstrates 'a variety of scenes with non-diffuse surfaces'; NeLT's summary lists diffuse and glossy illumination, dynamic shadowing and indirect illumination, with quality 'comparable to the recent advanced real-time denoiser'. Neither abstract makes a claim about sharp sender lobes onto diffuse receivers.
entries.cost_claims: NeLT: interactive rendering for dynamic scenes. Neural Radiosity: efficient synthesis of arbitrary views after the solve.
entries.limitation: Only abstracts were read; no information here on failure cases, rank or angular resolution.
entries.relevance: The nearest neural counterparts found from this angle: one replaces the fixed finite-element basis with an adaptive learned one but stores a solution, not an operator; the other stores per-object operators that survive rigid rearrangement.

implications: Exclusivity of a transport split is a property of path classes, not of estimators: a partition is exact when every path is assigned to exactly one class by the types of its vertices (Heckbert / Veach full-path expressions). The classical exclusive splits are (a) by vertex type - D-to-D transfer including intervening S* chains is stored, the trailing S*E chain is traced from the eye; (b) by the first non-specular vertex from the light - LS+D (caustic) is carried by a light-side pass, the rest by a gather; (c) by path length - k scattering events traced, the remainder stored. Each is exclusive only for a binary D/S material model.

Glossy lobes are neither D nor S. For them the split is a convention (a roughness threshold or a lobe-wise weight) that must be applied identically by both sides of the partition; otherwise energy is double counted or lost. The literature treats near-specular as 'more problematic' than ideal specular because it escapes the mechanisms built for the latter (Jakob & Marschner).

Veach's Theorem 8.3: local sampling can generate a path iff it contains a DD edge. A specular vertex forces one neighbour to be produced by sampling its BSDF. A receiver-side gather of a sharp sender violates this in the limit: the receiver's rays are chosen independently of the sender's lobe, so the hit probability scales with the lobe's solid angle. Every classical multi-pass system assigned light -> specular -> diffuse to a pass that samples the reflector's lobe from the light side (extended form factors, light ray tracing, caustic photon maps, particle tracing).

A stored table read at a path vertex makes that vertex behave as a D-type connection at the table's resolution. In the terms of path-space regularisation, a direction bin is a mollifier of fixed bandwidth: its bias is a blur of the bin width and does not vanish with more samples or more training.

The light transport operator on radiance is not compact, even for Lambertian scenes (Soler, Molazem, Subr 2022). Finite-rank or non-adaptive finite-basis approximations cannot bound error uniformly over light distributions; only pointwise (per-lighting) convergence is assured. A source-independent operator on a fixed patch x direction basis is in the class the theorem covers. The exitance operator fails to be compact where its kernel is unbounded: concave abutting edges, corners, contact points.

Rank is bounded below by a space-bandwidth product. Local dimensionality grows linearly with patch area with slope of the order of the BRDF (or shadow) bandwidth (Mahajan et al.), and as region size times bandlimit in the spatio-spectral concentration analysis (Lessig & Fiume). A global low-rank factor can hold broad transport over large regions or sharp transport over small ones, not sharp transport over large ones.

Required sampling density is predictable from local quantities: the sender BRDF's angular cutoff, surface curvature (which shears angular into spatial frequency and creates caustics), incidence angle, and inverse distance to blockers (Durand et al.). Bandwidth is unbounded at contact. Halving a lobe's width roughly quadruples the angular samples needed on the sphere.

Importance (the adjoint) determines how much stored error is visible. A diffuse reader integrates the table over a hemisphere and tolerates local error; a near-mirror reader is a point evaluation that assigns all its importance to a few entries. Classical glossy finite-element methods were affordable only because refinement was driven by a specific light and a specific view; an operator that is both source-independent and reader-independent forgoes that adaptivity.

In the operator factorisation, local scattering is spatially local and independent of scene layout; only the geometric propagation / visibility factor changes under a rigid edit. Classical dynamic methods exploit this by indexing the stored operator by the lines it integrates over (shafts, line-space hierarchy) and invalidating only entries whose line sets the moving object enters or leaves. That machinery was demonstrated for diffuse links; for non-diffuse transport the precedent (Granier & Drettakis) re-shoots particles instead of updating an operator.

Moving visibility out of the operator (antiradiance) makes pairwise links depend only on the two endpoints and therefore local under rigid edits, but occlusion then has to be reproduced by cancelling directional quantities at the resolution of the angular basis, the unoccluded operator can create energy, and convergence is not guaranteed for mirror-like BRDFs (eigenvalues above one were observed in 2D examples).

The sharp sender -> receiver relation through an ideal reflector is a finite, discrete set of geometric solutions per endpoint pair (Fermat paths; specular manifolds), with intensity given by wavefront curvature. It is determined by geometry alone and remains computable after any rigid edit without stored state; its cost is root finding per connection and grows with chain length and number of solutions. This is the 'full transport' price for that family against which any stored representation is measured.

Complexity claims for hierarchical operators (O(n) links, linear-time wavelet methods, O(p) glossy clustering) are stated for smooth kernels or for a fixed directional resolution. They do not include the growth of angular resolution with lobe sharpness; the naive glossy count is O(n^3) element triples, and many-light methods report needing several times more rows and columns once glossy transport enters the matrix.

Visibility discontinuities and glossy lobes are two distinct sources of high rank. Discontinuity meshing shows shadow edges are located by source x occluder geometry; the compactness analysis states that visibility discontinuities are not what breaks compactness (unbounded kernels and the partial-integral structure are); Mahajan et al. find cast shadows raise dimensionality roughly as the square root of area and glossy lobes linearly. A representation can therefore fail on one and not the other.

An operator pays off economically when it is reused across many right-hand sides (many lights, many frames) and the kernel compresses; the diffuse precedents (hierarchical radiosity, H-matrix view factors, direct-to-indirect transfer) meet both conditions. No source found here reports a compressed, source-independent operator that carries sharp glossy interreflection and is also reused across geometry edits.
closest_precedents: Extended form factors (Wallace et al. 1987; Sillion & Puech 1989): a geometry-only, source-independent linear operator between diffuse patches whose entries already include transfer via ideal specular chains, obtained by tracing through the mirrors per patch pair. Static scenes; ideal specular only.

Directional finite-element radiance (Immel et al. 1986; Sillion et al. 1991; Christensen et al. 1996/1997): the patch x direction (bins, spherical harmonics or 4D wavelets) representation with a linear transfer operator between such elements - structurally the same object as a patch x direction-bin table driven by a linear operator. Affordable only with light- and view-driven adaptive refinement; sharp lobes moved to ray-traced passes.

Three-point transport (Aupperle & Hanrahan 1993): radiance indexed by sender-receiver element pairs with hierarchical refinement of element triples, so that angular resolution follows geometry and BRDF instead of a fixed bin set.

Direct-to-indirect transfer (Hasan, Pellacini, Bala 2006; meshless hierarchical variant by Lehtinen et al. 2008): a precomputed, source-independent linear operator applied to an encoding of direct light to give multi-bounce indirect light, wavelet-compressed. Static geometry; broad sender radiance.

Line-space hierarchy for moving objects (Drettakis & Sillion 1997) and its glossy successor (Granier & Drettakis 2001): a stored hierarchical diffuse operator kept valid under object motion by invalidating only links whose shafts are crossed; non-diffuse transport handled by a separate incremental particle trace rather than by the operator.

Implicit visibility / antiradiance (Dachsbacher et al. 2007): a spatial x directional link operator made independent of third-party occluders, so only links touching the moved object change; low-frequency glossy only, stability not guaranteed for sharp BRDFs.
Modular Radiance Transfer (Loos et al. 2011): low-rank transport operators attached to shapes, reused and connected through interfaces after rearrangement; low-frequency diffuse indirect light only.

Many-light transfer matrix (Hasan et al. 2007; virtual spherical lights 2009): the receiver x virtual-light matrix as a per-frame, low-rank-sampled operator; documents the rank increase caused by glossy transport and the blur needed to control it.

Hierarchical low-rank view-factor matrices (Potter et al. 2022): a compressed source-independent diffuse operator reused over many illumination states with linear-scaling application cost; static geometry.

Neural counterparts seen from this angle (abstract level only): Neural Radiosity (Hadadan et al. 2021) replaces the fixed basis by a network but stores a per-scene solution, not an operator; NeLT (Zheng et al. 2023) stores per-object neural light transfer that is composed across objects in dynamic scenes. Other surveys in this series presumably cover neural precedents in depth; none was examined in full here.
unverified_or_uncertain: Confidence labels: 'read_primary_source' means the paper text was extracted and the quoted statements were located in it (Veach thesis section 8.3; Soler et al. 2022; Durand et al. 2005; Mahajan et al. 2007; Lessig & Fiume 2010; Dachsbacher et al. 2007; Kaplanyan & Dachsbacher 2013; Jakob & Marschner 2012; Zeltner et al. 2020; Christensen et al. 1996 and 1997; Lightcuts 2005; virtual spherical lights 2009). For those, only the passages relevant to this angle were read, not every section. All other entries rest on an abstract (official or archive page) or on a search-result summary of the abstract; mechanism details beyond the abstract in those entries are recalled from memory and are marked as such where they matter.

Heckbert 1990: the abstract page does not show the L(S|D)*E notation; the attribution rests on Veach's thesis ('Heckbert's regular expression notation') and course material, not on reading the 1990 paper's body.

Smits, Arvo, Salesin 1992 (importance-driven radiosity): the archive page had no abstract; the description comes from a search-result summary of the Cornell copy. The Cornell graphics server refused direct connections during this survey, so the Cornell-hosted PDFs for this paper, Arvo-Torrance-Smits 1994 and Sillion et al. 1991 were not read.

The same applies to the body of Drettakis & Sillion 1997 (abstract read on the SIGGRAPH history archive; the '2-3 frames per second' figure appears only in a search summary; the diffuse-only scope is inferred from the hierarchical-radiosity framing).
Lischinski, Tampieri, Greenberg 1992 (discontinuity meshing): bibliographic details and a one-paragraph description from search results; the IEEE page was not fetched.

Durand et al. 2005: the bandwidth bound (equation 20) was garbled by text extraction; only its stated dependencies (BRDF cutoff, curvature, normal-view angle, distance, harmonic mean of blocker distance) are reported, not the formula. The 'infinite bandwidth at contact points' remark is from the authors' project-page FAQ.
Aupperle & Hanrahan 1993: the O(n log n) claim is from the Stanford abstract; a second archive copy of the abstract is garbled and a Princeton tech-report copy is a draft.

Dachsbacher et al. 2007: two different DOIs appear in indexes (10.1145/1276377.1276453 and 10.1145/1239451.1239512); not resolved. The PDF URL given is the INRIA-hosted copy that was downloaded and read.

NeLT: indexes list ACM TOG 42(5), 2023; the SIGGRAPH history archive lists presentation at SIGGRAPH 2024. Only a four-sentence abstract was read; statements about glossy handling come from a search-result summary.
