That Arvo showed specular reflection makes the operator non-compact is taken from Soler et al. 2022's description.

Potter et al. 2022: the abstract does not discuss occlusion or block rank; the remark that off-diagonal blocks are not necessarily numerically low rank comes from a search-result summary of the paper body.

Works known or cited but not verified in this survey, and therefore not given entries: Arvo, 'Backward Ray Tracing' (SIGGRAPH 1986 course notes; only secondary descriptions found); George, Sillion, Greenberg, 'Radiosity Redistribution for Dynamic Environments' (1990; search did not return it); Forsyth, Yang, Teo 1994 and Shaw 1997 on hierarchical radiosity for dynamic environments (from memory); Pellegrini 1999 (cited by the antiradiance paper as the earlier visibility-free rendering equation; not read); Dmitriev, Brabec, Myszkowski, Seidel, 'Interactive Global Illumination Using Selective Photon Tracing' (EGWR 2002; search summary only, project page returned 403); Soler & Sillion, 'Hierarchical Instantiation for Radiosity' (2000; search summary only, venue unconfirmed); Chen & Arvo, 'Theory and Application of Specular Path Perturbation' (TOG 19(4), 2000; search summary only); Schroeder & Hanrahan, 'Wavelet Methods for Radiance Computations' (EGWR 1994; search summary only); Stamminger et al., three-point clustering for radiance computations (from memory); Kontkanen et al., 'Wavelet Radiance Transport for Interactive Indirect Lighting' (EGSR 2006; bibliographic entry only); Lehtinen et al. 2008 meshless hierarchical representation (abstract read, no entry); Bagher et al. 2012 bandwidth prediction and Belcour et al. 2013 5D covariance tracing (abstract or search summary only); Georgiev et al. / Hachisuka et al. 2012 vertex connection and merging (not searched successfully); Shirley 1990 'A Ray Tracing Method for Illumination Calculation in Diffuse-Specular Scenes' (citation only); Hanika et al. 2015 manifold next-event estimation (known only through Zeltner et al.'s description).

No source located in this survey states a quantitative bound of the form 'N receiver-side rays resolve a sender lobe of width w with error e' for interreflection; the nearest results are the Durand et al. sampling criterion (single bounce, image space) and the dimensionality results of Mahajan et al. and Lessig & Fiume (direct transport). Extending them to the light -> sharp reflector -> diffuse family is an inference, not a cited result.

The statement in the implications that no source reports a compressed source-independent operator carrying sharp glossy interreflection across geometry edits is a statement about what this survey found for this angle, not a proof of absence; precomputed radiance transfer for dynamic scenes and recent neural methods were outside this angle and were not searched systematically.

angle: Runtime caches and real-time global-illumination competitors (irradiance/radiance caching, photon maps and final gathering, probes, voxel cone tracing, online neural caches, ReSTIR GI/PT, path guiding, surfel / surface / hash caches, many-light methods): what each stores, what a rigid object move invalidates and how fast it recovers, how glossy / specular indirect light is treated, and published cost numbers. 30 entries; 21 were read in the primary source (PDF text extracted locally or full HTML), 9 at abstract / secondary level.

entries.work: Ward, Rubinstein, Clear - A Ray Tracing Solution for Diffuse Interreflection (irradiance caching)
entries.mechanism: Indirect illuminance is computed by hemisphere Monte Carlo sampling only at sparse surface points chosen during rendering, stored, and interpolated over surfaces in place of an ambient term; deeper bounces use proportionally fewer samples.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing learned. A lazily built, view-driven set of irradiance records (scalar/RGB irradiance at a point), reused across views of a static scene.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Formally nothing: every record whose hemisphere saw the moved object or its shadow/bounce is wrong, and the classic algorithm has no invalidation test. The common practice reported by Gautron (course notes) is full recomputation per frame, which wastes work and flickers because record positions change.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Excluded from the cache. Only the diffuse indirect term is cached; specular components are traced separately (Jensen 1996 notes that Radiance path-traces glossy surfaces).
entries.cost_claims: Abstract claims only qualitative savings (computation restricted to visible areas, reuse across views, fewer samples at deeper bounces).
entries.limitation: Irradiance has no directional content, so it cannot feed a glossy receiver; static-scene assumption.
entries.relevance: Origin of the 'sparse gather + interpolate' cache. Establishes that the classic economical cache works precisely because it discards the directional relation the project needs to keep.

entries.work: Krivanek, Gautron, Pattanaik, Bouatouch - Radiance Caching for Efficient Global Illumination Computation
entries.mechanism: Extends irradiance caching to cache incoming radiance as (hemi)spherical-harmonic coefficients, with translational gradients and rotation of coefficients; the glossy integral becomes a dot product with BRDF coefficients.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Per-BRDF hemispherical-harmonic tables (order adapts per outgoing direction, max order 10 in the examples) computed before rendering; radiance records (about 3.6 kB each at order 10) created lazily.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Records are reused across camera motion in a static scene (164 extra records for a second view). No geometry-edit handling in this paper; a moved object invalidates the records that see it.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Explicitly excluded. 'Radiance caching is not used for high-frequency BRDFs since many coefficients would be needed'; those are importance-sampled, and perfect specular uses one deterministic ray. The paper also states: 'radiance caching, as a gathering technique, cannot solve certain types of light transfer phenomena, such as caustics.'
entries.cost_claims: 2.2 GHz Pentium 4: indirect glossy term 33.3 s with 600 records versus 35 s for 12-ray importance sampling at much higher noise; animation 4.9 s/frame versus 35 s/frame (about 7x) in the Cornell box; 15 s versus 27 s/frame on the curved-surface scene.
entries.limitation: Restricted to low-frequency BRDFs (tested lobes were 'near the limit'); curved glossy receivers reduce reuse and need costly alignment; gathering cannot do caustics.
entries.relevance: Directly names the failure the project observed: a receiver-side gathering cache with a fixed angular basis cannot represent light -> sharp reflector -> receiver transport, and the directional budget grows with lobe sharpness.

entries.work: Gautron, Bouatouch, Pattanaik - Temporal Radiance Caching (read via Gautron's 2008 irradiance-caching course chapter)
entries.mechanism: Each cache record gets a temporal weighting function and temporal gradients; a record is reused over a validity interval estimated from the predicted change of incoming lighting (by reprojection), instead of recomputing the cache per frame.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing learned. Records plus an estimate of next-frame incoming radiance and temporal gradients.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Records far from the change keep an unbounded lifespan if their environment is static; records affected by motion get a short lifespan (user cap 'such as 5 to 10 frames'). Record positions are kept fixed over time to avoid flicker. Requires predefined animation (future frame known).
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Inherits radiance caching's low-frequency restriction; not addressed further in the text read.
entries.cost_claims: Qualitative 'significant speedup' and reduced flicker in the chapter read; no numbers extracted.
entries.limitation: Thresholds set by trial and error; temporal gradients are first order and smooth fast changes; 'ghost' artifacts from obsolete records; needs knowledge of the next frame.
entries.relevance: Shows the classical answer to 'what does a rigid move invalidate': a per-record validity time derived from measured lighting change, i.e. a transport-dirty set estimated physically rather than a retrained model.

entries.work: Jensen - Global Illumination using Photon Maps (caustic map + global map + final gathering)
entries.mechanism: Two light-traced photon maps: a high-resolution caustics map (photons emitted toward specular objects, stored on diffuse hits) visualised directly, and a low-resolution global map used only as an approximate radiance estimate after a diffuse bounce and to guide sampling in a distribution ray tracer.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing learned. 200,000-500,000 photons per test scene, in a kd-tree; source dependent.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not addressed; both maps are scene- and light-specific and are rebuilt for a changed scene (see Dmitriev 2002 for selective update).
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Split by path family. Specular and highly glossy reflection seen by the eye: Monte Carlo ray tracing. Caustics (light -> specular -> diffuse): 'We never compute caustics via Monte Carlo sampling since this is almost impossible in most situations' - they come only from the light-traced caustics map. The approximate global-map lookup is used only after a diffuse reflection or beyond a distance threshold; radiance estimates from the map are 'limited to surfaces ranging from Lambertian to slightly glossy'.
entries.cost_claims: Glossy Cornell box about 7x faster than Radiance; photon count affects render time only slightly.
entries.limitation: Density-estimation blur and bias; memory in photons; no dynamic-scene mechanism.
entries.relevance: The tested mechanism (exact 1-2 events, table lookup at the second camera vertex) has the same structure as final gathering over a global map, and this paper already states the two rules the failure violated: the approximate store may only be read through a diffuse/wide footprint, and the light -> specular -> diffuse family must be carried by a separate light-side estimator.

entries.work: Dmitriev, Brabec, Myszkowski, Seidel - Interactive Global Illumination Using Selective Photon Tracing
entries.mechanism: Quasi-Monte Carlo photon tracing with density estimation on a mesh; photons are grouped using the periodicity of the Halton sequence so that a few 'pilot' photons that hit a moving object identify whole groups of coherent 'corrective' photons to re-shoot (negative energy for the old state, positive for the new).
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing learned. A photon pool partitioned into groups; illumination bucketed on mesh elements.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: All photon groups whose pilots did not intersect the moved object (or its previous position, the 'scene phantom') are kept; only invalid groups are re-traced, prioritised by pilot hits and view visibility. Detection is explicitly not conservative.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Out of scope: 'In this paper we focus on global illumination for diffuse environments'; the authors note hierarchical radiosity poorly supports glossy/specular transfer.
entries.cost_claims: 8 fps (ROOM) and 1.1 fps (HOUSE) on a dual 1.7 GHz P4 with a GeForce3; update converges progressively over iterations.
entries.limitation: Mesh-based reconstruction of indirect light (coarse); probabilistic invalidation can miss affected photons; diffuse only.
entries.relevance: A purely physical precedent for selective recomputation after a rigid move: a geometry-indexed partition of light paths, a cheap probe that identifies the transport-dirty subset, and exact reuse of the rest - without any learned state.

entries.work: Yang, Ouyang - Real-Time Ray Traced Caustics (adaptive anisotropic photon scattering)
entries.mechanism: Photons are traced from the light through metallic / transparent surfaces each frame, splatted with anisotropic footprints from photon differentials, and a negative-feedback loop redistributes photon density toward regions near the camera or temporally unstable in screen space.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing precomputed or learned; per-frame photon buffer plus light-space feedback buffers.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Stated as fully dynamic with no preprocessing: the estimator is recomputed each frame; only the feedback (density) state carries over and re-adapts.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: This is its sole purpose: caustics from highly polished metallic and transparent objects after multiple bounces are produced light-side, then shaded on the receiver (GGX shading pass using the receiver G-buffer).
entries.cost_claims: Described as low cost; a per-GPU timing table exists (RTX 2060 to 3090, 1080p/1440p) but I could not extract it reliably.
entries.limitation: Screen-space driven (targets visible receivers); denoiser dependent; I read only the introduction and parts of the method.
entries.relevance: Shows what real-time practice does for the exact family that broke the learned operator: emit from the light side with adaptive density, rather than gather from the receiver side.

entries.work: McGuire, Mara, Nowrouzezahrai, Luebke - Real-Time Global Illumination using Precomputed Light Field Probes
entries.mechanism: A grid of octahedral probes stores radiance, normals and radial distance (plus filtered irradiance and distance moments); world-space rays are marched through the probes' depth maps in a shader to fetch radiance with correct visibility, for diffuse and glossy gathers.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Precomputed probes (e.g. a 4^3 grid of 1024x1024-texel probes), 8 bytes/texel uncompressed; nothing learned.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Static environments only; dynamic objects can receive but the probes are not updated. A geometry edit requires re-rendering the probes.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Handled by ray marching into radiance probes, with a stated resolution rule: to avoid aliasing on perfect mirrors, probe texel solid angle must not exceed the pixel's solid angle at the probe centre. Second- and higher-order mirror reflections are 'viewpoint biased according to probe locations'.
entries.cost_claims: Living-room global illumination in 4.7 ms.
entries.limitation: Precomputed and static; higher-order specular parallax error; probe resolution scales with the lowest roughness in the scene.
entries.relevance: A physically computed cache that does keep sharp directional relations - at the price of probe resolution tied to mirror sharpness and no validity under geometry edits.

entries.work: Majercik, Guertin, Nowrouzezahrai, McGuire - Dynamic Diffuse Global Illumination with Ray-Traced Irradiance Fields (DDGI); and Majercik et al. - Scaling Probe-Based Real-Time Dynamic Global Illumination for Production (2021, arXiv 2009.10796)
entries.mechanism: A probe grid stores low-resolution octahedral irradiance and depth moments; every frame each probe traces a few rays against the current scene and blends results with hysteresis; multi-bounce comes from shading probe rays with the previous frame's probes. The 2021 paper adds probe states (sleeping/awake), adaptive hysteresis and cascades.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing precomputed or learned; 8x8-texel irradiance and depth per probe, updated online.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Nothing is declared valid; all values relax toward the new solution by exponential blending (hysteresis 0.85-0.98, i.e. a time constant of roughly 7-50 frames by my arithmetic), with a further one-frame-per-bounce lag. 2021: expanded bounding boxes of dynamic objects wake sleeping probes; probes are not repositioned around dynamic objects; scene-change events temporarily lower hysteresis for all probes.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Not cached. First-order glossy/specular reflection is ray traced per pixel; at second-hit surfaces the glossy energy is folded into the matte term (2019), and second-order reflections are forced to maximum roughness (2021).
entries.cost_claims: 6 ms/frame versus 1 min/frame path traced (RTX 2080 Ti, 1080p). Table 2: indirect diffuse total 2.6 ms for 32x8x32 probes x 64 rays, plus 2.4 ms for brute-force ray-traced glossy. 2021: probe sleeping saves 30-50 % on average.
entries.limitation: Diffuse-only cache; temporal lag and ghosting with small bright lights; leak handling by heuristics; hysteresis heuristics act globally.
entries.relevance: The canonical physically computed cache that survives rigid edits without retraining. It delivers the broad-transport saving at 2-3 ms with tens of frames of lag, and its authors chose to exclude sharp glossy transport from the cache altogether.

entries.work: Rodriguez, Leimkuhler, Prakash, Wyman, Shirley, Drettakis - Glossy Probe Reprojection for Interactive Global Illumination
entries.mechanism: Paths with multiple glossy interactions are stored in precomputed light probes with an adaptive parameterisation (more resolution for shinier surfaces and complex geometry) and reprojected per view using reflection estimation and a rasterisation-based search; probes are precomputed at lower roughness and an adaptive bilateral filter restores the true roughness at runtime.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Precomputed glossy probes plus light maps for diffuse; nothing learned.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Static scenes with opaque objects only; a geometry edit requires recomputing the probes.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Central topic: multi-glossy-bounce paths are baked into probes; parallax at occlusion boundaries would sharpen reflections, addressed by the two-step roughness split.
entries.cost_claims: Interactive rates 'fitting in the memory, bandwidth, and computation constraints of current hardware' (abstract only).
entries.limitation: Static geometry and lighting; memory grows with shininess.
entries.relevance: Evidence that a cache holding sharp multi-glossy interreflection has been built only as a static precomputation with resolution that adapts to shininess - there is no dynamic-geometry counterpart in this survey.

entries.work: Crassin, Neyret, Sainz, Green, Eisemann - Interactive Indirect Illumination Using Voxel Cone Tracing
entries.mechanism: Direct light is injected into the leaves of a sparse voxel octree storing pre-filtered geometry, incoming radiance and Gaussian-lobe normal distributions; final gathering is approximated by tracing a few cones through the mip hierarchy (several diffuse cones plus one specular cone whose aperture follows the specular exponent).
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Static octree built once (about 280 ms); nothing learned.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: The static part of the octree persists (time-stamped); animated objects are re-voxelised every frame (about 5.5 ms/frame for a 16K-triangle mesh) and radiance is re-injected and re-filtered each frame.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Glossy handled as one pre-filtered cone (example 10 degree aperture); storing incoming rather than outgoing radiance permits glossy senders, but voxel averaging limits sharpness and causes leaking (the 'two red-green wall' problem). Mirror-sharp interreflection is not claimed.
entries.cost_claims: 25-70 fps on a GTX 480; 32 ms versus 37 ms for light propagation volumes at 512^2; roughly 1024 MB video memory, 'especially due to the support for indirect specularity'.
entries.limitation: Two bounces; visibility is approximate (opacity averaging, leaks); memory.
entries.relevance: A geometry-indexed, pre-filtered cache where the angular footprint is explicit (cone aperture). It shows that narrowing the cone raises both cost (16.6 ms at 10 degrees versus 3.9 ms at 60 degrees for 3 AO cones) and memory.

entries.work: Wright, Narkowicz, Kelly - Lumen: Real-time Global Illumination in Unreal Engine 5
entries.venue: SIGGRAPH 2022 course, Advances in Real-Time Rendering in Games
entries.mechanism: Per-mesh 'cards' form a surface cache (material + direct + indirect lighting in an atlas) that secondary rays read; the first bounce is solved by a screen-space probe final gather (8x8 directional resolution) backed by a world-space radiance cache (32x32); multi-bounce comes from surface-cache feedback across frames; reflections have their own pipeline.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Cards and mesh distance fields are generated at mesh import (about 0.2 ms and 0.6 ms for a 1.5M-triangle mesh); lighting is entirely runtime; nothing learned.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Object-local data (cards, mesh distance fields) move with the object. Global distance field bricks are updated only where modified; surface-cache lighting is refreshed under a fixed texel budget per frame (1024^2 direct, 512^2 indirect) - 'fixed update cost, variable lighting latency'; history rejection gives 'slow reaction to lighting changes, which shows up as ghosting behind moving objects'. Skeletal meshes have no surface-cache parameterisation.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Banded by roughness: 0.4-1.0 resample the screen radiance cache (no reflection rays, 50-70 % cost reduction); 0.3-0.4 short ray then world radiance cache (32x32); below 0.3 dedicated reflection rays. Mirror reflections need hardware ray tracing and hit lighting; for mirror, cards would need to match screen pixel density; distance fields 'aren't perfect for mirror reflections'.
entries.cost_claims: 1080p internal: about 6.4 ms (High, 60 fps target) and 11.3 ms (Epic, 30 fps target) total on console for The Matrix Awakens, reflections 2.3 / 4.6 ms of that; surface-cache multi-bounce below 1/16 of Lumen's budget. The offline lighting build 'has a hundred thousand times more processing time'.
entries.limitation: Coarse voxel lighting in the surface cache; latency; skinned meshes; material response in the surface cache is approximated ('approximate specular and subsurface' by modifying albedo).
entries.relevance: The most complete shipped answer to 'cache what is broad, trace what is sharp'. It quantifies where a cache with fixed angular resolution stops being acceptable (roughness about 0.3-0.4) and shows object-local state surviving rigid motion while radiance values are amortised.

entries.work: Halen, Brinck, Hayward, Bei - Global Illumination Based on Surfels (GIBS)
entries.venue: SIGGRAPH 2021 course, Advances in Real-Time Rendering in Games
entries.mechanism: Surfels are spawned from the G-buffer onto visible geometry, persist, and accumulate ray-traced diffuse irradiance with a variance-tracking moving average; each surfel also stores depth moments for a Chebyshev visibility test.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing precomputed or learned ('no need for time consuming bakes').
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Surfel placement survives motion: each surfel stores a local position relative to a transform ID (rigid object or dominant skinning bone) and follows it every frame. Irradiance values are not declared valid; when a surfel sees its mean change it requests more rays and re-converges, then returns to an 'almost dormant' ray count.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Out of scope: the method computes indirect diffuse only ('the BRDF we are dealing with is essentially the cosine lobe').
entries.cost_claims: About 7 ms total in a large-draw-distance scene; about 11 ms while converging in a 1,400-light stress case with a 1M ray budget; near-converged after 15 frames with 4-sample lightcut sampling; one example 'converged to acceptable quality in about five seconds'. Global ray budget is artist-set.
entries.limitation: Diffuse only; convergence time in many-light scenes; one-bone skinning approximation.
entries.relevance: Shows that 'state attached to the moving object stays valid under rigid edits' is cheap for the parameterisation, and that the radiance stored on it is re-estimated physically with a variance-driven budget - a non-learned selective recompute.

entries.work: Boisse, Meunier, de Dinechin, Bartels, Veselov, Eto, Harada - GI-1.0: A Fast Scalable Two-Level Radiance Caching Scheme for Real-Time Global Illumination
entries.mechanism: Level 1: screen probes (8x8 octahedral, one per 8x8 tile) store incoming radiance at primary vertices; level 2: a world-space spatial-hash cache stores outgoing radiance at secondary vertices; probe rays terminate in the hash cache; reservoir light sampling feeds it.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: No preprocessing, nothing learned.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Probes are reprojected with motion vectors and reused only if plane distance and normal agree; holes get reallocated rays; a shadow-preserving hysteresis adapts blend strength to the difference between new and reprojected radiance; hash cells decay when unaccessed. No latency figure is given.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Not delivered: glossy reflections are 'still in progress'; the plan is to sample GGX directions into the caches and to cast a ray for low roughness.
entries.cost_claims: 1.9-3.4 ms total for direct + indirect at 1080p with 1/4 sample per pixel (RX 6900 XT / RTX 3080); 2.4 ms versus 2.6 ms for Lumen in the authors' internal test.
entries.limitation: Infinite-bounce feedback only where the contributing surface was visible in the previous frame; light-grid clamping bias; no glossy.
entries.relevance: A recent, fully physical two-level cache with exactly the 'few exact events, then table lookup' structure of the tested mechanism. It reaches about 2-3 ms without learning, and still has no answer for glossy.

entries.work: Binder, Fricke, Keller - Massively Parallel Path Space Filtering
entries.mechanism: Contributions of path vertices that fall in the same jittered, quantised hash cell (position, normal, optionally more) are averaged, replacing neighbourhood searches by one hash lookup; works at non-primary vertices.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing; a hash table of per-cell averages maintained across frames.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: For static scenes averages converge; for dynamic environments two sets of averages are combined with an exponential moving average, and the paper shows that this blurs moving shadow boundaries while full temporal integration averages them out.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: 'On highly reflective surfaces ... filtering is pointless. Therefore, vertices on such surfaces should not be selected in the first place. On glossy surfaces, however, filtering may reduce variance efficiently, again at the cost of a certain bias.' Layered materials are filtered per layer with different keys.
entries.cost_claims: About 1.5 ms overhead at HD; 1 path per pixel plus filtering 'very closely approximates' a 1024-path reference in the shown scene.
entries.limitation: Biased; quantisation and light leaking; temporal adaptation versus integration trade-off.
entries.relevance: The physical analogue of a patch-indexed radiance table. Its authors state the selection rule for which vertices may read the table (not specular ones), and it costs about 1.5 ms.

entries.work: Pantaleoni - Online Path Sampling Control with Progressive Spatio-Temporal Filtering
entries.mechanism: A spatio-directional hash (position x outgoing direction for outgoing radiance; position x incoming direction for incoming radiance) is filled by filtering path samples with temporal feedback, described as a hybrid of progressive radiosity and path tracing; the approximation is used for importance sampling, control variates or a biased estimator.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing offline; online-estimated hash cells (48 bytes; 4M-entry table), optionally k-d tree or Gaussian-mixture guiding records.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Per-cell counters blend linear and exponential averaging with a maximum temporal window; counters 'can be reset locally, on demand, or globally after large structural changes'; the solver lags by about one frame per feedback step.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: The directional hash key exists specifically to encode 'directional variations like those due to glossy reflections', and the author reports reproducing glossy interreflections; caustics are stated as not handled by next-event estimation and needing other techniques.
entries.cost_claims: RTX 2080 Ti, 1080p, 1 spp: +2-4 ms on 16-20 ms of path tracing for the control-variate / biased estimators; guiding adds about 30-70 ms; k-d tree control variate about 13x faster than path tracing with NEE at equal variance.
entries.limitation: Bias constant chosen by hand; guiding overhead; not compared with offline guiding.
entries.relevance: The closest non-learned precedent to the tested table: a (patch x outgoing-direction) radiance store built progressively by physical transport with feedback. It attains glossy directionality by hashing direction at fixed resolution and updates under edits by counter resets.

entries.work: NVIDIA SHaRC - Spatially Hashed Radiance Cache (integration guide)
entries.mechanism: A world-space hash grid of voxels stores accumulated radiance; an update pass path-traces from a sparse subset of pixels (e.g. one per 5x5 block, about 4 % of paths) and back-propagates; rendering paths query the cache at every non-primary hit and terminate on success.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing; hash entries (8 B) plus accumulation and resolved buffers (16 B each); about 160 MiB for 2^22 entries, 256 MiB with SH directional encoding.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Values are blended over a maximum accumulated-frame count (higher = better quality, slower response); entries expire after a stale-frame limit; a 'responsive lighting' mode trades long-term accumulation for reaction speed. The guide does not discuss dynamic geometry specifically.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Guarded lookup: 'unlike diffuse lobes, specular ones should be treated with care' - the cache may be used only when the lobe's estimated cone spread, 2 x ray length x sqrt(0.5 a^2 / (1 - a^2)), exceeds the voxel size; otherwise the path continues. Optional SH encoding prevents highlights leaking to other view directions.
entries.cost_claims: No frame-time figures in the guide; occupancy 10-20 % for a static camera.
entries.limitation: Hash collisions; artifacts on short segments and glossy surfaces unless the spread checks are applied.
entries.relevance: States, as an engineering rule, the footprint condition under which a cached value may substitute for transport. A lookup at a near-mirror vertex fails this test by construction.

entries.work: Muller, Rousselle, Novak, Keller - Real-time Neural Radiance Caching for Path Tracing (NRC)
entries.mechanism: A small MLP (5 hidden layers x 64) maps position, direction, normal, roughness and reflectances to scattered radiance; paths are terminated into the cache once their area spread exceeds a threshold relative to the primary footprint (c = 0.01); the network is trained online each frame on self-bootstrapped targets.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: No pretraining ('pretrained networks would struggle to generalize to new dynamic scenes'); weights learned online from 65,536 records per frame, 4 gradient steps, EMA of weights 0.99.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Nothing is retrained offline, but the weights are continuously re-fitted; summarised from the paper: usable after about 8 frames and overall colours correct after about 64 frames from scratch. Old content is forgotten at the learning rate.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Roughness and direction are inputs, and the spread heuristic lengthens paths after sharp bounces so that 'cache artifacts are observed through rough reflections and therefore averaged out'. Sharp detail not carried by the inputs, 'such as a sharp contact shadow or caustic', is poorly captured.
entries.cost_claims: About 2.6 ms at 1080p (query 1.59 ms + training 1.11 ms on average); lower bias but higher variance and cost than DDGI.
entries.limitation: Low-frequency scintillation; self-training bias; slow or failed learning of shadows and caustics with small networks or noisy targets.
entries.relevance: The main learned competitor that needs no retraining step under rigid edits. It is source-dependent and scene-specific (radiance, not an operator), and it too only reads the cache through a wide footprint.

entries.work: Dereviannykh, Klepikov, Hanika, Dachsbacher - Neural Two-Level Monte Carlo Real-Time Rendering (Neural Incident Radiance Cache, NIRC)
entries.mechanism: An online-trained network predicts incident radiance at a vertex (queried many times, e.g. 25 neural samples); a two-level Monte Carlo estimator adds an unbiased path-traced estimate of the residual between cache and truth; a balanced termination heuristic decides where the cache may end a path.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Online-trained tiny MLP with multi-resolution hash features; no offline training.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Continuously re-fitted; in the dynamic Bistro test the method 'starts to outperform the standard Monte Carlo approach with the same compute budget after approximately 20 frames'.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Operates on up to 3 non-specular vertices; the termination heuristic is introduced 'acknowledging its limitations, particularly with glossy details'; the residual estimator keeps the result unbiased where the cache is wrong.
entries.cost_claims: One cache evaluation takes 2-25x less compute than a path-tracing sample.
entries.limitation: Residual variance where the cache is poor; warm-up frames after changes.
entries.relevance: Shows a way existing work bounds the damage of a wrong cached value at a sharp receiver: the cache is a control variate with a path-traced residual, so localised cache error appears as noise rather than as a biased reflection.

entries.work: Ouyang, Liu, Kettunen, Pharr, Pantaleoni - ReSTIR GI: Path Resampling for Real-Time Path Tracing
entries.mechanism: Each pixel keeps a reservoir holding one indirect sample (visible point, sample point, outgoing radiance at the sample point, random seed); samples are resampled across pixels and frames with a reconnection Jacobian.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing; screen-space reservoir buffers of fixed size.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Stored outgoing radiance becomes stale: 'temporal reuse may cause bias if the outgoing radiance values stored at the sample points become inaccurate ... the result may be a noticeable lag'. Mitigations: reservoir count clamps (30 temporal, 500 spatial), re-tracing stored samples for validation every 6 frames, and a shadow ray to the sample point.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Stated limitation: 'not effective with multi-bounce global illumination with highly glossy surfaces. Not only is our assumption of Lambertian scattering at sampled points inaccurate in that case, but spatial sample reuse will be much less effective since a sample point that makes a large contribution at one pixel may be outside the peak specular lobe of another.' Glossy receivers also worsen bias.
entries.cost_claims: RTX 3090, 1080p: 1-spp two-bounce path tracing 8.0 ms versus ReSTIR GI 8.9 ms (biased) / 9.6 ms (unbiased); MSE improvement 9.3x-166x over path tracing at one sample per pixel. The authors note games typically allow less than 2 ms for GI.
entries.limitation: Screen-space storage (disocclusion noise, perfectly specular objects); Lambertian assumption at the sample point; temporal lag.
entries.relevance: Its reconnection step is the same geometric operation as gathering a sender through a receiver-side ray; the authors give the same diagnosis as the project's failure - a sample valid for one receiver falls outside the narrow lobe for another.

entries.work: Lin, Kettunen, Bitterli, Pantaleoni, Yuksel, Wyman - Generalized Resampled Importance Sampling: Foundations of ReSTIR (ReSTIR PT); with Lin, Kettunen, Wyman - ReSTIR PT Enhanced (2026)
entries.mechanism: Full paths are reused between pixels and frames through shift mappings: reconnection where the vertices involved are rough enough, random-number replay through glossy/specular vertices (hybrid shift), with lobe-specific connectability. The 2026 paper replaces fixed roughness/distance thresholds by ray-footprint criteria and halves spatial-reuse cost.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing; 88-byte reservoirs per pixel (reconnection vertex + replay seed).
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Nothing is assumed valid: reused paths are re-evaluated (shifted) in the current scene, so the estimator stays unbiased/consistent; the temporal confidence cap 'avoids slow sample turnover in dynamic scenes'.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Explicitly addressed. Reconnection is allowed only when the lobes at the three vertices exceed a GGX roughness of about 0.2 and the segment is long enough; otherwise the path is re-traced by random replay. 'Reconnection shifts ... often fail to reconnect on near-delta BRDFs.' Contact caustics reuse well with the hybrid shift; caustics from distant small highlights perform poorly with it; sharp caustics can still be undersampled ('noise, streaks, or splotches'). A manifold-exploration shift is named as future work.
entries.cost_claims: RTX 3090, 1080p: reconnection 5 ms versus hybrid 12 ms in the glossy Cornell box; full prototype 'originally 40-80 ms per frame'; the enhanced version is 2-3x faster (37.1 -> 12.6 ms in its Figure 1, from a search snippet).
entries.limitation: Screen-space undersampling of tiny geometry / very high-frequency light; correlation artifacts in glossy scenes with hard lighting; cost.
entries.relevance: The strongest current evidence on how sharp directional relations are reused without bias: not by storing radiance, but by storing the path and re-deriving the constrained vertex (replay), with an explicit roughness/footprint gate deciding where a stored connection is admissible.

entries.work: Kettunen, Lin, Ramamoorthi, Bashford-Rogers, Wyman - Conditional Resampled Importance Sampling and ReSTIR
entries.mechanism: Extends GRIS to conditional path spaces so that path suffixes can be reused conditioned on non-reused prefixes; the prototype is a ReSTIR PT with a final-gather pass that postpones reuse by at least one bounce.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing; suffix reservoirs.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: As ReSTIR PT: reused suffixes are re-evaluated; no persistent validity claim.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Not stated in the abstract; the motivation is that, 'as in photon mapping, such a final gather reduces blotchy artifacts from sample correlation'.
entries.cost_claims: None in the abstract; the code repository describes the prototype as very costly (recommends an RTX 4090).
entries.limitation: Cost; abstract-level reading only.
entries.relevance: Confirms that 'exact prefix + reused suffix behind a final gather' is the current frontier form of the tested mechanism's structure, done with resampled paths instead of a table.

entries.work: Muller, Gross, Novak - Practical Path Guiding for Efficient Light-Transport Simulation (SD-tree); with Vorba et al. 2014 - On-line Learning of Parametric Mixture Models for Light Transport Simulation
entries.mechanism: An approximation of the incident radiance field is learned online (spatial binary tree x directional quadtree; or Gaussian mixtures trained from a stream of particles) and used only as a sampling density for scattering directions, with automatic budgeting between training and rendering.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Per-scene, per-lighting incident-radiance distributions learned during rendering (Vorba: e.g. 30 training passes within a one-hour render).
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not addressed (offline, static scenes); the learned distributions are scene- and light-specific and would have to be re-learned.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Demonstrated on 'complex specular-glossy light transport'; because the learned field only steers sampling, errors in it raise variance but do not bias the image.
entries.cost_claims: No fixed numbers in the abstracts; training cost is said to be amortised by better sampling.
entries.limitation: Directional resolution of the guide limits how well narrow features are found; memory; learning time.
entries.relevance: Establishes the alternative role for a learned or cached transport representation - as a proposal distribution rather than as the answer - under which a localised error at a mirror cannot appear as a wrong reflection.

entries.work: Dittebrandt, Hanika, Dachsbacher - Temporal Sample Reuse for Next Event Estimation and Path Guiding for Real-Time Path Tracing
entries.mechanism: A world-space octree whose leaves hold a visibility light cache (lights with unoccluded samples) and a compressed directional quadtree (32-128 bits) for guiding; both, and the octree itself, are adapted every frame from the previous frame's path samples.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: No precomputation ('must not require precomputation exceeding the budget within one frame'); per-leaf sampling structures adapted online.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Structures are incrementally adapted from last frame's samples; for dynamic surface points whose current leaf is empty a fallback is used; an exploration technique keeps the estimator unbiased while the guide is stale.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Not specifically; the directional quadtree is most useful with strong contribution from a specific direction (e.g. the sun) and gives no benefit under uniform illumination.
entries.cost_claims: Update and rebuild of all structures about 1 ms; about 6 ms added to path tracing at 1080p; MSE reduced by at least an order of magnitude in many situations.
entries.limitation: Very low directional resolution; scene-dependent benefit.
entries.relevance: A real-time, dynamic-scene instance of guiding: a stale directional cache costs variance only, and re-adaptation takes one frame of samples and about 1 ms.

entries.work: Keller - Instant Radiosity; Kollig, Keller - Illumination in the Presence of Weak Singularities (bias compensation)
entries.mechanism: Light subpaths are traced from the sources and their vertices become virtual point lights (VPLs); indirect light is the sum of direct lighting from VPLs with shadow maps. Contributions are clamped to remove 1/r^2 and narrow-lobe spikes; Kollig and Keller restore the clamped energy with an unbiased path-traced term.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing learned; a set of VPLs plus one shadow map each, specific to the light and scene.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not addressed in the originals; any VPL whose light path or shadow map sees the mover is invalid (see Laine 2007).
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Classical VPLs are diffuse-only and clamped; as characterised by Hasan et al. 2009, 'light bouncing off glossy surfaces is ignored' and clamping loses glossy energy; the compensation term in glossy scenes can cost nearly as much as path tracing the whole image (3.5 hours in the VSL paper's example versus 34 s for the clamped render).
entries.cost_claims: See above (secondary).
entries.limitation: Clamping bias; compensation degenerates to path tracing when the missing energy is significant.
entries.relevance: The many-light formulation is the sender-side dual of receiver-side gathering and fails at the same place: a narrow lobe makes single connections spiky, and removing the spikes removes real energy that is expensive to restore.

entries.work: Laine, Saransaari, Kontkanen, Lehtinen, Aila - Incremental Instant Radiosity for Real-Time Indirect Illumination
entries.mechanism: Single-bounce indirect light from a few hundred VPLs whose paraboloid shadow maps are reused across frames; only a few VPLs (4-8 of 256) are replaced per frame to keep a good distribution as the primary light moves.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: No precomputation; persistent VPLs and shadow maps.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Validity relies on static bouncing geometry: 'We require that the geometry used for bouncing off indirect illumination remains static. Dynamic objects cannot [bounce light]' but can receive it; VPL validity is checked by a shadow ray against the static scene only.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Diffuse only; the authors note that with highly specular BRDFs the contributions of individual VPLs would become more [uneven], i.e. the approach degrades for sharp lobes.
entries.cost_claims: 49 fps at 1024x768 with 256 VPLs on an 80K-triangle scene; 31 fps with 1024 VPLs versus 2 fps for the comparison method; up to 7x faster.
entries.limitation: 'Perhaps the biggest limitation ... indirect illumination can bounce from static geometry only'; single bounce; not view-driven.
entries.relevance: A clean example of cache reuse whose validity condition is exactly 'the sender geometry did not move' - the asymmetry (movers receive but do not send) is the cheap half of dynamic GI.

entries.work: Walter, Fernandez, Arbree, Bala, Donikian, Greenberg - Lightcuts: A Scalable Approach to Illumination
entries.mechanism: Point lights (including VPLs) are clustered in a binary light tree; for each shading point a cut through the tree is chosen so that the bounded approximation error stays below a perceptual threshold.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: The light tree, built per frame/scene; nothing learned.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not addressed (offline); the tree depends on light and VPL positions and would be rebuilt.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: The abstract claims 'non-diffuse materials' at the receiver; cluster error bounds depend on the receiver BRDF, so sharper lobes force deeper cuts. Senders remain VPLs.
entries.cost_claims: Strongly sublinear: hundreds of thousands of point lights approximated with a few hundred shadow rays, tens with reconstruction cuts.
entries.limitation: Inherits VPL clamping and diffuse-sender limits (per Hasan 2009); abstract-level reading only.
entries.relevance: A physically computed, error-bounded hierarchical approximation of the receiver <- many senders sum; it shows the cost of the gather can be made sublinear in senders without learning, but not that narrow sender lobes are resolved.

entries.work: Hasan, Pellacini, Bala - Matrix Row-Column Sampling for the Many-Light Problem
entries.mechanism: Transport is viewed as a large matrix of sample-light interactions whose column sum is the image; a small number of full rows and columns, rendered on the GPU with shadow maps, reveals the matrix structure and yields a reduced set of representative lights.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing learned; a reduced (low-rank-like) approximation of the transfer matrix computed per frame from sampled rows and columns.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not addressed; the sampled rows/columns contain visibility and would be recomputed.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Abstract claims 'arbitrary shaders'; glossy sender transport still depends on the VPL formulation (addressed later by VSLs, which reuse this algorithm).
entries.cost_claims: Light transfer computed 'within a few seconds' for scenes with indirect and environment illumination.
entries.limitation: Abstract-level reading; quality depends on the matrix being close to low rank.
entries.relevance: A direct non-learned precedent for obtaining a compact approximation of the transport matrix by physically sampling a few rows and columns (compare: a generator fed stratified visibility rays emitting low-rank factors).

entries.work: Hasan, Krivanek, Walter, Bala - Virtual Spherical Lights for Many-Light Rendering of Glossy Scenes
entries.mechanism: Each virtual light's contribution is integrated over a non-zero solid angle (a sphere around the light-path vertex) using both BRDFs, removing the spikes from narrow glossy lobes and the 1/r^2 term, so no clamping is needed; rendered with matrix row-column sampling.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Nothing learned; up to about 250,000 VSLs per image (limited by reduced-matrix memory).
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Not addressed (offline, per image).
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Central topic. The paper states prior many-light methods 'are incorrect for two reasons': diffuse-only VPLs ignore light bouncing off glossy surfaces, and clamping removes energy. Using the full glossy BRDF at a point VPL 'does not help either, since even more clamping has to be applied'. VSLs preserve most glossy effects but blur some lighting features.
entries.cost_claims: High-quality images in 1-4 minutes (GPU) where path tracing references took 2.2-316 hours on 8 cores; Kollig-Keller compensation 3.5 hours and photon mapping 1 hour on the motivating example.
entries.limitation: Biased but consistent (converges as VSL count grows and radius shrinks); blur; memory cap on VSL count.
entries.relevance: Shows the known price of making a finite sender set carry glossy-to-glossy transport: angular integration at both ends, with blur proportional to the support - narrow lobes are regularised, not resolved.

entries.work: Diolatzis, Philip, Drettakis - Active Exploration for Neural Global Illumination of Variable Scenes
entries.mechanism: A neural generator renders a variable scene from first-hit G-buffers plus an explicit vector of scene parameters (object positions/rotations, materials, lights); training data are path-traced renderings chosen by a Markov-chain exploration of the parameter space.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: One network per variable scene, trained 5-18 hours on an RTX 6000 (under an hour when specular bounces are ray traced at runtime).
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: Valid without retraining only for edits inside the trained parameterisation (the declared variables and their ranges, including moving objects); anything else requires retraining.
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Learns all paths including glossy reflection and caustics, but 'high-frequency effects, such as sharp mirror reflections, may not be reproduced exactly'; the authors suggest a hybrid with real-time ray tracing for specular interactions.
entries.cost_claims: 4-6 fps at 900x900 on an RTX 3090 in an unoptimised prototype.
entries.limitation: Per-scene; scaling in the number of variables (128 variables already loses some shadows and highlights); source-dependent output.
entries.relevance: A learned competitor that does survive rigid edits without retraining - by enumerating them at training time - and that also hands sharp specular transport back to ray tracing.

entries.work: Zeng, Dong, Peers, Wu, Tong - RenderFormer: Transformer-based Neural Rendering of Triangle Meshes with Global Illumination
entries.mechanism: Rendering as sequence-to-sequence: triangle tokens with reflectance go through a view-independent transformer stage modelling triangle-to-triangle light transport, then a view-dependent stage turns ray-bundle tokens into pixel patches.
entries.what_is_precomputed_or_learned: Transformer weights learned once across scenes; 'does not require per-scene training or fine-tuning'.
entries.what_stays_valid_under_geometry_edits: By construction any edit is a new input sequence, so no retraining; the whole forward pass is re-run. Light sources are part of the token set (not a source-independent operator applied afterwards).
entries.handling_of_sharp_glossy_interreflection: Abstract claims evaluation on 'scenes with varying complexity in shape and light transport'; no specific claim on sharp glossy interreflection in what I read.
entries.cost_claims: None in the abstract; a secondary summary reports a limit of 4,096 triangles.
entries.limitation: Scale (token count); no physical guarantees stated in the abstract; abstract-level reading only.
entries.relevance: The closest published instance of a learned, geometry-conditioned, cross-scene transport model with an explicit view-independent transport stage; it bounds what has been shown (small scenes, no operator-level linearity/passivity contract).

implications: The path family that failed (light -> sharp reflector -> diffuse patch) is the LS+D caustic family, and its failure under receiver-side gathering is documented prior art rather than a property of the learned operator: Krivanek 2005 states that radiance caching 'as a gathering technique, cannot solve ... caustics'; Jensen 1996 never computes caustics by Monte Carlo gathering and carries them in a separate light-traced map; GRIS 2022 reports sharp caustics as an undersampling failure of reuse; ReSTIR GI states that a sample contributing strongly at one receiver lies outside the peak lobe of another.

Every cache in this survey that is read by a path guards the read with a footprint or roughness test, and a lookup at a near-mirror second vertex violates all of them: Jensen (approximate estimate only after a diffuse bounce or beyond a distance threshold), NRC (area-spread termination), SHaRC (cone spread must exceed the voxel size), path space filtering (specular vertices 'should not be selected'), Lumen (screen cache only for roughness 0.4-1.0, world cache for 0.3-0.4, rays below 0.3), DDGI (second-order glossy forced to maximum roughness), ReSTIR PT (reconnection only above GGX roughness of about 0.2).

No surveyed runtime cache stores sharp glossy interreflection in a form that survives a geometry edit. The two systems that do cache sharp multi-glossy transport (light field probes 2017, glossy probe reprojection 2020) are precomputed and static, and both tie storage resolution to the sharpest lobe (probe texel solid angle <= pixel solid angle for mirrors; more resolution for shinier surfaces). Lumen makes the same statement for its surface cache (mirror reflections need cards at screen pixel density).

For broad (diffuse and rough-glossy) transport, physically computed caches with no learned parameters already deliver the saving at published costs of roughly 1.5-3.5 ms per 1080p frame on 2019-2022 GPUs (path space filtering 1.5 ms; DDGI 2.6 ms diffuse + 2.4 ms ray-traced glossy; NRC 2.6 ms; GI-1.0 1.9-3.4 ms) and 6-11 ms for a complete production system including reflections (Lumen). A learned operator restricted to broad transport is competing against those numbers.

What those physical caches do not provide is instant validity: after a rigid move their stored radiance is wrong and relaxes over frames (DDGI hysteresis 0.85-0.98; ReSTIR GI validation every 6 frames and reservoir clamp 30; NRC about 8 frames usable / 64 frames for correct colours; NIRC about 20 frames; GIBS about 15 frames near-converged; Gautron record lifespans 5-10 frames; Lumen 'fixed update cost, variable lighting latency' with ghosting behind movers). Any economic comparison therefore has to state whether the target is steady-state cost per frame, lag after an edit, or error during the transient.

All runtime caches surveyed store source-dependent radiance or irradiance, not a source-independent operator; a light change invalidates them just as a geometry change does. Source independence plus zero-lag validity after a pose change are the properties a geometry-conditioned operator offers that these caches do not, and the operator's cost of regenerating factors per pose (visibility rays plus network inference) is the quantity to set against the caches' per-frame ray budgets.

Rigid motion preserves object-attached state at near-zero cost in shipped systems (GIBS surfels follow a transform ID; Lumen cards and mesh distance fields are per mesh; acceleration structures refit), while everything that encodes inter-object visibility or received radiance is recomputed. Laine 2007 shows the cheap asymmetric case: moving objects may receive cached indirect light but may not send it.

Physical precedents for selective recomputation exist without learning: Dmitriev 2002 identifies invalid photon groups with pilot photons and re-shoots only those (non-conservatively); Gautron 2007 assigns each record a validity interval from measured lighting change; Lumen updates only modified distance-field bricks and a budgeted subset of cache pages; Pantaleoni 2020 resets cell counters locally.

For sharp transport the prior art's economic lever is sampling, not storage: ReSTIR PT re-derives the constrained vertex by random replay and remains unbiased; path guiding uses a learned or cached field only as a proposal density; NIRC adds a path-traced residual to a cached value. In all three a wrong cached value at a sharp receiver becomes variance. A table lookup, as in ReSTIR GI's Lambertian-sample assumption or a radiance cache, turns the same error into a biased, visibly localised reflection.

Removing narrow-lobe energy from a finite-sample formulation and compensating elsewhere has a documented price: VPL clamping loses glossy energy; unbiased compensation approaches the cost of path tracing in glossy scenes (3.5 hours versus 34 s in the VSL paper's example); the VSL remedy integrates over a solid angle and blurs. A low-rank global term that compensates for a near-zero single-flight term is in the same position as clamping plus compensation.

Angular resolution is the cost driver wherever directional radiance is cached: Krivanek's records are about 3.6 kB at harmonic order 10 and still cannot represent Lafortune exponents of 88-186 accurately; voxel cone tracing costs 16.6 ms at a 10 degree cone versus 3.9 ms at 60 degrees and spends about 1 GB largely on indirect specular; Lumen needs 8x8 directions for rough and 32x32 for mid-glossy lobes. A fixed patch x direction-bin table inherits this scaling.

Even ReSTIR PT, the method that most directly targets glossy and specular reuse, reports that reconnection fails on near-delta BRDFs, that caustics from small distant highlights are poorly handled by its hybrid shift, and that its prototype cost 40-80 ms per frame on an RTX 3090 before the 2026 optimisations (2-3x faster). Sharp glossy interreflection under real-time budgets is not a solved problem that a new method merely has to match.

Published 'cheaper than path tracing at matched quality' claims in this area are stated as equal-time error ratios (ReSTIR GI: 9.3x-166x MSE at about +1 ms over an 8 ms 1-spp frame; Pantaleoni: about 13x at equal variance; Dittebrandt: >= 10x MSE) or as time-to-quality with a denoiser. The reference cost of 1-spp two-bounce path tracing at 1080p on an RTX 3090 is about 8-19 ms in those papers.
closest_precedents: Hasan, Pellacini, Bala 2007 (matrix row-column sampling): a physically computed low-rank-style approximation of the sample x light transport matrix from a few sampled rows and columns - the non-learned counterpart of 'visibility rays in, low-rank factors out'. Per frame, source-dependent, not geometry-generalising. https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~kb/projects/rowcolumnSampling

Pantaleoni 2020 (progressive spatio-temporal filtering): a (position x outgoing-direction) hashed radiance table built by progressive-radiosity-like feedback of path samples - the closest physically computed analogue of the tested patch x direction-bin table, including glossy directionality. Source-dependent; updated by counter resets. https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.07547

Jensen 1996 (global photon map + final gathering, separate caustic map): same two-tier structure as the tested mechanism (exact first events, approximate store read after a wide bounce), with the LS+D family routed to a separate light-side estimator. https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall14/cos526/papers/jensen96.pdf

Zeng et al. 2025 (RenderFormer): learned, geometry-conditioned, cross-scene, with an explicit view-independent triangle-to-triangle transport stage; lights are tokens rather than an input to a separate linear operator; small scenes. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21925

Diolatzis, Philip, Drettakis 2022 (Active Exploration): learned generator conditioned on explicit rigid-pose parameters, valid without retraining inside the trained range; per-scene, source-dependent, sharp mirror reflections not exact. https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.08272

Ren et al. 2024 (LightFormer, SIGGRAPH 2024): neural many-light formulation - each light generates VPLs encoded into a neural light representation, composited per pixel by attention; claims fully dynamic scenes in real time. Read at project-page level only; glossy handling and generalisation to unseen scenes not confirmed. https://wylighting.github.io/lightformer

Muller et al. 2021 (NRC) and Dereviannykh et al. 2025 (NIRC): learned radiance (not operator), trained online, so valid under any edit after a warm-up of roughly 8-64 frames; NIRC adds an unbiased residual. https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.12372 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04634

Hadadan, Chen, Zwicker 2021 (Neural Radiosity, arXiv 2105.12319): a network represents the full radiance field by minimising the rendering-equation residual; per-scene optimisation, handles non-diffuse surfaces per the abstract; Su et al. 2024 (Dynamic Neural Radiosity, SIGGRAPH Asia 2024) extends it to variable scenes with an explicit scene vector (search-snippet level only). https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.12319

Dmitriev et al. 2002 (selective photon tracing): not learned, but the closest precedent for a geometry-indexed partition of transport with a cheap probe that identifies the dirty subset after a rigid move. https://www.graphicon.ru/oldgr/en/publications/text/spt.pdf

Precomputed transport operators applied to the current direct illumination in a static scene are cited by Laine et al. 2007 as a separate category ('precompute transport operators that are used at runtime ... in a static scene'); that family (PRT, direct-to-indirect transfer) was outside this angle and is not surveyed here.
unverified_or_uncertain: I found no published runtime cache that retains sharp glossy interreflection under geometry edits; this is absence of evidence within one search session, not a proof that none exists.

ReSTIR PT Enhanced: the 37.1 ms -> 12.6 ms figure comes from a search snippet of the paper's Figure 1; from the PDF text I confirmed only '2-3x faster' and 'originally 40-80 ms per frame on an RTX 3090'. Year is 2026 (PACMCGIT 9(1)), although the task brief's field may know it as 2025.

Lumen numbers were extracted from slide-note text with imperfect table alignment; the association of 6.38 / 11.31 ms totals and 2.30 / 4.62 ms reflections with The Matrix Awakens on console rests on the accompanying sentence ('On High settings the total Lumen cost is 6.4 milliseconds, while Epic ... 11.3'). The hardware for that table was not unambiguous in the extracted text.

GIBS timings (about 7 ms, about 11 ms in a stress case, 15 frames, 'about five seconds') are from slide notes without a consolidated table; hardware not extracted. I found no statement on glossy in the slides beyond the diffuse-only scope.
DDGI convergence in frames (about 7-50) is my conversion of the published hysteresis range 0.85-0.98 to an exponential time constant, not a number stated in the paper.

NRC adaptation figures ('usable after about 8 frames (~70 ms)', 'overall colours correct after the first 64 frames') come from an automated summary of the ar5iv full text; I did not locate the sentences myself.

NIRC: per-frame timings in its teaser (e.g. path tracing 41.2 ms versus biased variant 37.9 ms) were visible in extracted text but I could not map them to scenes/hardware with confidence, so they are omitted from the entry.
RenderFormer's 4,096-triangle limit is from a search summary, not from the abstract I read.
Keller 1997 (Instant Radiosity) and Kollig & Keller 2004 were not read directly; their content is taken from descriptions in Hasan et al. 2009 and search summaries.

Ward 1988: only the abstract page was read; the statement that specular components are traced separately is supported indirectly (abstract mentions 'diffuse and specular components'; Jensen 1996 says Radiance path-traces glossy surfaces).
Gautron et al. 2007 was read through the author's 2008 course chapter, not the TVCG paper; no speedup numbers extracted.
Real-Time Ray Traced Caustics (RTG2 ch. 30): a timing table exists but did not extract cleanly; no numbers reported.

Ritschel et al. 2008, Imperfect Shadow Maps (SIGGRAPH Asia 2008): verified to exist; reported as fully dynamic VPL-based indirect illumination at 19 fps on a GeForce 8800 GTX (project-page snippet). Glossy support not confirmed; the MPI page returned 403. Not included as an entry.

Boisse 2021, World-Space Spatiotemporal Reservoir Reuse (SIGGRAPH Asia 2021 Technical Communications): PDF read; implemented for single-bounce diffuse GI only; a performance table exists but values did not extract. Folded into the GI-1.0 lineage rather than given its own entry.
Dachsbacher et al. 2014, Scalable Realistic Rendering with Many-Light Methods (CGF 33(1)): existence and scope verified; its discussion of glossy limitations was not read.
Walter, Khungurn, Bala 2012, Bidirectional Lightcuts: seen only in a search snippet (claims gloss handling); not read.

Zeltner, Georgiev, Jakob 2020, Specular Manifold Sampling (SIGGRAPH 2020): abstract fragments only; relevant as the deterministic-connection alternative for reflective caustics, not surveyed in depth.

Recalled from memory and not verified in this session: Tawara, Myszkowski, Seidel 2004 (temporal coherence in final gathering); Smyk et al. 2005 (temporally coherent irradiance caching); Walter et al. 1999 Render Cache and Tole et al. 2002 Shading Cache; Tabellion & Lamorlette 2004 (cited inside Laine 2007 and the Lumen notes, not read); Enlighten runtime radiosity; Embark's Kajiya renderer; AMD Brixelizer GI; Sannikov's Radiance Cascades; Kaplanyan & Dachsbacher 2010 light propagation volumes (cited in the VCT paper as the comparison baseline).

The LuxCoreRender forum summary claiming ReSTIR GI 'cannot handle caustics' is a secondary source; the paper itself states the glossy multi-bounce and Lambertian-sample limitations quoted in the entry.
Cost numbers span hardware from a 2002 dual Pentium 4 to an RTX 3090 and are not normalised; cross-entry comparisons are indicative only.
